question: What is the main difference between an inflammatory joint disease and osteoarthritis?
explanation: Think of inflammatory joint diseases as the immune system mistakenly attacking the joint lining (synovitis), while osteoarthritis is simply the wear and tear of cartilage as we age. Spotting this difference helps you understand why they are treated differently! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h1)

question: In inflammatory joint conditions, what is 'pannus'?

options.A: An abnormal tissue layer that destroys cartilage and bone
options.B: Fluid accumulation in the outer layer of the skin
options.C: Thickened scar tissue formed after a surgical incision
options.D: A hard calcium crystal deposit inside the joint space

explanation: Pannus is an extra layer of bad, granulation-like tissue that grows inside the joint and slowly eats away at the cartilage and bone. You'll often see this in conditions like rheumatoid arthritis! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h1)

question: How do joints usually get affected in rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: Restricted entirely to the spinal column
options.B: Limited to a single weight-bearing joint
options.C: Symmetrical across both sides of the body
options.D: Randomly scattered without any clear pattern

explanation: A classic sign of rheumatoid arthritis is symmetry! If the left wrist or knee hurts, the right one is usually acting up in the exact same way. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h2)

question: A client with rheumatoid arthritis wakes up with severe joint stiffness that lasts for nearly two hours. What does this tell you as a nurse?

options.A: It represents normal muscle fatigue from daily exercise
options.B: It indicates active and ongoing systemic inflammation
options.C: It suggests the client is experiencing a sudden bone fracture
options.D: It points to a localized soft tissue injury from a fall

explanation: Morning stiffness that drags on for an hour or more is a major red flag for active inflammation inside the joints. Great nursing assessment catches this early! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h2)

question: Which substance builds up in the joints to trigger a painful gout attack?
explanation: Gout happens when excess uric acid forms sharp, needle-like crystals (monosodium urate) in the joint space. Ouch! That's what causes that sudden, intense pain. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h3)

question: What is the medical term for the hard bumps of urate crystals that form under the skin in long-standing gout?
explanation: Tophi are those visible lumps of uric acid crystals that can pop up under the skin or around joints when gout isn't well controlled over time. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h3)

question: Which genetic marker is closely linked with ankylosing spondylitis?
explanation: Keep this gene in mind: HLA-B27 is strongly tied to ankylosing spondylitis, a condition that mainly stiffens up the spine. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h4)

question: What major change happens to the spine in advanced ankylosing spondylitis?

options.A: Cartilage between discs completely dissolves and leaks
options.B: Vertebrae fuse together into a rigid structure
options.C: Spinal nerves swell and permanently pinch the spinal cord
options.D: Bones become overly soft and prone to micro-fractures

explanation: Over time, chronic inflammation causes the small bones of the spine (vertebrae) to grow together and fuse, making the spine completely rigid like a bamboo stick. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h4)

question: Which two blood tests do doctors frequently order to check for general inflammation in the body?
explanation: ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate) and CRP (C-Reactive Protein) are your go-to blood markers for spotting inflammation anywhere in the body. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h5)

question: When assessing a joint with active inflammation, what physical signs do you expect to find?

options.A: Complete absence of pain during active body movement
options.B: Local warmth and swelling around the affected joints
options.C: Unilateral muscle hypertrophy near the inflamed area
options.D: Cool, pale skin directly over the affected joint spaces

explanation: Inflamed joints get hot and swollen because extra blood rushes to the area. Trust your hands when you palpate—warmth is a classic sign of trouble! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h5)

question: Why are DMARDs prescribed for clients with inflammatory joint diseases?

options.A: To provide instant pain relief during a severe acute flare
options.B: To rebuild lost cartilage within the damaged joint space
options.C: To slow down disease progression and joint damage
options.D: To permanently cure the underlying autoimmune response

explanation: DMARDs (Disease-Modifying Anti-Rheumatic Drugs) don't just mask pain; they step in to slow down the immune attack and protect the joints from long-term destruction. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h6)

question: A client taking long-term NSAIDs for joint pain reports stomach upset and dark, tarry stools. What should you do first?

options.A: Advise the client to double the fluid intake immediately
options.B: Report the findings promptly to the healthcare provider
options.C: Suggest taking the medication on an entirely empty stomach
options.D: Reassure the client that dark stools are a normal side effect

explanation: Dark, tarry stools are a telltale sign of bleeding in the gut (GI bleed), a serious side effect of long-term NSAID use. Always report this right away! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h6)

question: Which exercise choice is safest and best for a client with an inflammatory joint disease?

options.B: High-impact running on hard asphalt surfaces

explanation: Low-impact activities like swimming let clients stay active and keep their joints flexible without pounding them with heavy mechanical stress. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h7)

question: When is it best to apply cold packs instead of heat to an inflamed joint?

options.A: When the client is experiencing prolonged morning stiffness
options.B: During an acute inflammatory flare with active swelling
options.C: Just before the client begins a daily stretching routine
options.D: To help relax tight muscles surrounding a chronic joint

explanation: Cold constricts blood vessels, which works wonders for calming down fresh swelling and numbing sharp pain during an acute flare-up. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h7)

question: Why are people with chronic inflammatory joint conditions at higher risk for heart problems?

options.A: Lack of physical movement directly stops the heart from pumping
options.B: Joint pain triggers constant adrenaline surges that damage valves
options.C: All anti-inflammatory medications cause immediate cardiac arrest
options.D: Systemic inflammation accelerates atherosclerosis and heart disease

explanation: When the body is constantly fighting inflammation, it speeds up the hardening of blood vessels (atherosclerosis), which puts extra stress on the cardiovascular system. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h8)

question: A client with rheumatoid arthritis on long-term steroids lifts a light bag and suddenly feels sharp back pain. What complication should you suspect?

options.A: A vertebral compression fracture due to bone weakening
options.B: An acute flare of ankylosing spondylitis in the lower spine
options.C: A minor muscle strain that will resolve with resting in bed
options.D: A systemic infection spreading rapidly through the bloodstream

explanation: Long-term steroid use weakens bones (causing osteoporosis), making clients very vulnerable to sudden spinal compression fractures from even minor movements like lifting. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h8)
